extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors seeking traditional publishing and literary representation (writers querying agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and behavioral standards for writers who want to be traditionally published or represented by a literary agent, covering querying, readiness, professional conduct, career resilience, and preparation. Drawn from Janet Reid's 'Rules for Writers' (agent perspective).

rubrics_metrics.name: BE BOLD
rubrics_metrics.description: Query widely; there’s no single right answer and no 'Query Police' — if an agency member said no to a full, unless told not to, query other agents including at the same agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: Query Widely rather than over-researching whether you're 'allowed' to query. Agents are always looking for good projects; don't be afraid of offending agents. Anti-patterns: excessive fretting about etiquette that prevents querying. Notes: If you spend too much time worrying you’ll miss opportunities; treat querying as proactive and confident.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE BRAVE
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept and seek hard experiences (e.g., attending conferences, having your pages read aloud, receiving blunt criticism) and persist instead of collapsing or quitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two parts: (1) bravery to invest time/money and show up (travel, pitch sessions), (2) bravery to hear criticism and act on it. Practical: take notes, don't give up after harsh feedback, go home and revise. Anti-patterns: immediate despair or quitting after critique; letting one bad panel or rejection stop you.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE COMMITTED
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat writing and a publishing career as a craft and long-term business — build and participate in community, attend author events, and be persistent in improving craft and platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do: write the best book you can, query widely, publicize your work after publication, support peer authors at bookstores, cons, festivals. Build community by participating (author events, conventions). Read long-term history of publishing to get perspective (example recommendation given). Anti-patterns: retreating from community or expecting overnight success.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE CONFIDENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Let your writing demonstrate your talent rather than asserting credentials; you are a writer regardless of publication status — show, don't tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on self-reported claims (e.g., 'I was nominated for an Edgar' will be checked). Confidence = allow manuscript/query to prove your case. Anti-patterns: over-explaining, depending on third-party claims instead of strong writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE IMPERFECT
rubrics_metrics.description: Make lots of mistakes as part of learning; avoid paralysis from fear of mistakes and instead iterate and learn from failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: thick skin from rejections, learning what works, moving forward creates chance. Specific actions encouraged: query broadly (query everyone), re-query up to 3 times if you get no response (updated guidance: try again twice more), bring query/manuscript where you might meet agents, write outside your comfort zone. Anti-patterns: being rude or stupid (those are mistakes you shouldn't make), repeating the same mistakes without learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE KNOWLEDGABLE
rubrics_metrics.description: Know your field and market: research similar books, read widely in your genre, and be realistic about claims that 'there aren't any books about this'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong prescription: if you haven't read at least ~100 books in your area, you're likely not ready. Practical: search Amazon for comparable titles, read trade reviews and genre magazines, keep a reading list, check publisher catalogs. Anti-patterns: claiming uniqueness without evidence — Reid double-checks such claims and will reject if wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE POLITE
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat all publishing staff (especially non-agent assistants) with respect; rudeness to office staff is an immediate route to rejection or being 'fired'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: assistants perform essential, irreplaceable tasks and their opinions matter. Anti-patterns: being mean or rude to support staff; such behavior is unforgivable and counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE POSITIVE
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a constructive, positive attitude toward feedback and setbacks; accept compliments, process criticism, and focus on strategy rather than self-doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical: when you get a compliment, accept it; when sales are poor, grieve briefly then strategize with your agent. Anti-patterns: disbelieving positive feedback and letting self-doubt immobilize you. Emotional regulation (shake off panic and move to action) is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE RATIONAL
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume every rejection or form response is about you personally; consider many non-personal reasons an agent might pass on material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of 'it's about me': agent not enamored of topic, overwhelmed with work, turf issues, or similar projects already on the list. Practical: don't catastrophize over form rejections; engage your thinking brain rather than reptilian panic. Anti-patterns: personalizing every negative response.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE REACHABLE
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your contact information works and that you can be contacted (working email, site with contact info).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bounced emails prevent agents from following up. Maintain a visible, reliable contact point (author website, bio with email or contact page). Anti-patterns: providing nonfunctional email addresses or being hard to contact when an opportunity arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE READY
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared for unexpected opportunities: carry pages/first chapter, have materials accessible at conferences, be ready if an agent asks for pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tips: keep manuscript pages in your car, hotel room, purse; attend workshops on pitching so you're prepared; being ready can lead to impromptu readings and agent interest. Anti-patterns: being unprepared when asked for pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE RESOLUTE
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on what you can control (writing the best book) rather than obsessing over hypotheticals; reinventing a career is possible but individualized and should be handled with an agent when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: stop gnawing on 'what ifs' and concentrate on writing and querying. Career reinvention has no template — it depends on sales, category, goals, and timing. Anti-patterns: planning for disasters before they happen; paralysis by speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE TENACIOUS
rubrics_metrics.description: Persist despite beliefs that publishing is closed to newcomers; agents and publishing need new authors and persistence can overcome lack of connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter myths: agents don't already have all the clients they need; editors work through agents and agencies still seek new talent. Practical: keep writing, keep querying, build perseverance. Anti-patterns: giving up because you don't know the 'right people' or aren't in NYC.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE WARY
rubrics_metrics.description: Vet prospective agents: ask what they have sold and which editors they know who might like your book; be cautious of agents without industry connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific screening questions: 'What have you sold?' and 'Which editor might like my book?' Rationale: an agent without editorial contacts is less useful. Anti-patterns: accepting representation without checking the agent's network or sales record.

rubrics_metrics.name: BE YOURSELF
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain personal authenticity but be deliberate about what personal material you publish or include in queries; don't hide or fake yourself to please unknown gatekeepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical: don't include links to highly personal blog content in a query letter; decide what to reveal and when. Be aware of potential stigma (example discussed: mental illness) but prioritize your writing and honesty. Anti-patterns: oversharing in professional contexts, or erasing yourself to fit perceived expectations; both can harm career and creativity.
